nameStory: Yellow iris gets its common name from its bright golden-yellow flowers and sword-like leaves that resemble the mythical iris, named after the Greek goddess of the rainbow. It's also called 'water flag' because it waves like a banner near streams and ponds, while 'yellow flag' comes from the Old English meaning of flag as a rush or reed-like plant.
description: Yellow iris is a tall, showy wetland perennial that looks like it belongs in a fancy garden but grows wild in New England's marshes and pond edges. It reaches 3-4 feet tall with dramatic sword-shaped leaves that fan out from the base like a green fountain. In late spring and early summer, it produces stunning bright yellow flowers with three large drooping petals and three smaller upright ones, creating an unmistakable iris shape that's hard to miss.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with classic iris shape - three large drooping petals (falls) and three smaller upright petals (standards), blooming in late spring to early summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, sword-like leaves up to 3 feet long that feel firm and smooth, with a prominent ridge down the middle that you can run your finger along

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms large clumps in wet areas, growing 3-4 feet tall with leaves fanning out from the base in a fountain-like arrangement

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Large, three-chambered seed pods that split open to reveal brown seeds, often persisting into winter as dried, papery capsules

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Always found with 'wet feet' - growing directly in water or soggy soil that squishes underfoot, never in dry upland areas

habitat: Yellow iris thrives in New England's wetlands, growing along pond shores, stream banks, marshes, and wet meadows where the soil stays consistently moist or waterlogged. You'll often find it forming large colonies in shallow water or boggy areas, sometimes mixed with cattails, sedges, and other water-loving plants. It tolerates both full sun and partial shade but needs that constant moisture to flourish.

seasonality.spring: New green sword-like leaves emerge early, followed by dramatic yellow flower spikes in late spring that are impossible to miss against the wetland backdrop.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade by mid-summer, leaving tall green foliage that remains lush and prominent throughout the growing season, with seed pods beginning to develop.
seasonality.fall: Leaves start to yellow and die back while large, three-chambered seed pods ripen and split open, revealing brown seeds that float away on water.
seasonality.winter: Most foliage dies back to ground level, but you might spot dried seed pods still standing above the snow or ice in frozen wetlands.

funFact: Yellow iris is such an aggressive spreader that it's actually considered an invasive species in much of New England - a single plant can form a colony covering several acres within just a few years by sending out underground stems called rhizomes!
confusionNotes: The sword-like leaves might remind you of cattails before they flower, but iris leaves have that distinctive ridge down the middle and feel much firmer and smoother. Sweet flag also has similar leaves, but yellow iris leaves are typically wider and the flowers are completely different - sweet flag has tiny, inconspicuous brown flower spikes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its beauty, yellow iris is actually a non-native species that escaped from colonial gardens and naturalized throughout New England's wetlands. The name 'pseudacorus' means 'false sweet flag' because early botanists noticed the leaves looked similar to sweet flag (Acorus calamus), though the two plants aren't related at all.
compareHints: Yellow iris is the only consistently yellow-flowered iris you'll find growing wild in New England wetlands - all our native iris species like northern blue flag have blue or purple flowers. While other iris species might occasionally have pale or white forms, none produce the bright golden-yellow blooms that make this species unmistakable. The wetland habitat also sets it apart from garden irises that prefer drier soil.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern blue flag is much larger and more robust than slender blue flag, which has narrow, grass-like leaves and smaller flowers.
Japanese Iris differs from Northern Blue Flag by its gray-green (rather than bright green) leaves and reddish-purple flower tones instead of pure blue-purple.
Slender blue flag is much more delicate than the common northern blue flag, with leaves that are dramatically narrower (pencil-width vs.

Unlike its freshwater-loving cousins like northern blue flag (which grows in marshes and pond edges), beach-head iris is the only New England iris that can survive in pure beach sand with constant salt exposure.
Dwarf crested iris is dramatically smaller than all other New England irises - while northern blue flag and yellow iris tower at 2-4 feet tall in wetlands, this woodland species stays under 6 inches.
Unlike New England's native blue flag irises which are tall wetland plants, netted iris is tiny and prefers dry, well-drained soils.
Compared to northern blue flag, southern blue flag typically has broader, more rounded flower petals and slightly wider leaves.
Unlike other New England irises that have blue, purple, or yellow flowers, blackberry lily is the only one with orange, spotted blooms.
Sweet iris differs from New England's native blue flag irises by its sweet fragrance and slightly more purple-tinted flowers.
Siberian iris differs from Northern Blue Flag by having much narrower, more grass-like leaves and more compact growth, while Yellow Iris has broader leaves and bright yellow flowers.
Japanese iris differs from native blue flags by its massive, completely flat flowers and preference for consistently wet, acidic soil.
Unlike our common northern blue flag with its blue-purple flowers or the invasive yellow iris with bright yellow blooms, cemetery iris stands out with pure white flowers.
